text:
Code






Target trial emulation  ·  NZAVS 2018–2023  ·  Lab report
Religious Attendance: Selective, Not Sweeping
Target trial emulation shows that supported causal effects of religious attendance on well-being are selective
Joseph A. Bulbulia · Don E. Davis · Crystal Park · Kenneth G. Rice · Geoffrey Troughton · Daryl R. Van Tongeren · Chris G. SibleyEvolutionary Human Sciences · 2026

Religious service attendance is associated with better well-being, but observational associations do not establish causation. Across six annual waves of a national panel, we estimate the causal effects of monthly attendance on 24 well-being indicators — and the supported effects concentrate in meaning, forgiveness, and intimate life, with little change in somatic health, psychological distress, or social support.


  46,377participants at baseline, NZAVS
  6annual waves, 2018–2023
  24well-being indicators
  2–3%of non-attenders initiate attendance per year



The emulated trial

  
    What is our question?
    For New Zealand adults, what are the causal effects of monthly religious service attendance on 24 well-being indicators, measured across somatic, psychological, existential, social, and relational domains?
  
  
    What is our population?
    46,377 NZAVS participants at baseline, followed across six annual waves, 2018–2023. The primary contrast concerns the 38,477 who were not attending at baseline, with censoring adjustment carrying inference to that cohort.
  
  
    What interventions do we compare?
    
      Fails positivity
      Make everyone attend monthly, versus none. Only 2–3% of non-attenders initiate attendance in a given year; the data cannot identify a policy this far from what occurs.
    
    
      Adopted · δ = 5
      Multiply each non-attender's chance of taking up monthly attendance fivefold, versus the natural course — the censoring-adjusted course actually observed.
    
  




The central result
Small, supported gains appear in meaning and purpose, forgiveness, and sexual satisfaction; distress and somatic health barely change.
Estimates come from the supported stochastic contrast above, fitted with a sequentially doubly robust estimator and cross-validated machine learning among baseline non-attenders.


  
    Supported · where attendance acts
    Meaning, forgiveness, intimacy
    Meaning and purpose rises by 0.085 standard deviations (E-value 1.25), sexual satisfaction by 0.086 (1.25), and forgiveness by 0.075 (1.21). Smaller supported gains appear for meaning and sense (0.071), short-form health (0.061), and body satisfaction (0.058).
  
  
    Null · where it does not
    Distress and the body barely change
    Body mass index, sleep, and alcohol use, and the distress indicators — anxiety, depression, fatigue, rumination — show point estimates near zero with confidence intervals spanning the null. Social belonging and perceived social support do not meet the E-value reliability threshold.
  




Inference & robustness

  
    01Estimation
    A sequentially doubly robust estimator with cross-validated machine learning adjusts for 62 baseline covariates and 32 time-varying confounders, with inverse-probability-of-censoring weights for dropout.
  
  
    02Sensitivity
    Each supported effect clears the study's E-value reliability threshold (E-values 1.16–1.25); an unmeasured confounder would need associations of that strength with both attendance and outcome to explain the effect away.
  
  
    03Measurement
    Attendance is self-reported, and measurement error in self-reports would pull estimates towards zero — actual effects may be larger than we report.
  
  
    04Scope
    We estimate total effects of specified changes in attendance rather than mediated pathways, and population averages rather than subgroup effects. Effects probably vary by tradition, belief strength, upbringing, and relationship status; childhood religious socialisation lies outside what adult panel data can identify.
  




  Citation
  Bulbulia, J. A., Davis, D. E., Park, C., Rice, K. G., Troughton, G., Van Tongeren, D. R., & Sibley, C. G. (2026). Target trial emulation shows that supported causal effects of religious attendance on well-being are selective. Evolutionary Human Sciences, 8, e16. doi:10.1017/ehs.2026.10043
  Data: the New Zealand Attitudes and Values Study. Estimation: supported stochastic interventions with a sequentially doubly robust estimator.

title: Resources
text:
Software and Tools

R Packages

Causal InferenceResearch Tools


margot A framework for causal inference with panel data, supporting doubly robust estimation and sensitivity analyses. Documentation is at go-bayes.github.io/margot, and the source code is at github.com/go-bayes/margot. Install with devtools::install_github("go-bayes/margot").
ggdag Create directed acyclic graphs for causal inference. Documentation is at r-causal.github.io/ggdag, and the CRAN page is cran.r-project.org/package=ggdag. Install with install.packages("ggdag").
WeightIt Weighting for covariate balance in observational studies. Documentation is at ngreifer.github.io/WeightIt, and the CRAN page is cran.r-project.org/package=WeightIt. Install with install.packages("WeightIt").


boilerplate Tools for generating standardised boilerplate text and documentation for reproducible research. Documentation is at go-bayes.github.io/boilerplate, and the CRAN page is cran.r-project.org/package=boilerplate. Install with install.packages("boilerplate").

text:
Reference Texts

Core Textbooks


Causal Inference: What If Miguel A. Hernan and James M. Robins Free Book and Resources. The definitive text on causal inference methods with code examples.

Explanation in Causal Inference Tyler VanderWeele Link to OUP page. A strong account of causal mediation analysis and interaction. The hardback is expensive, so a library copy is often the easiest option.




The Effect Nick Huntington-Klein Free Online. A practical guide with clear visualisations.




Additional Resources
Statistical Rethinking by Richard McElreath provides a Bayesian approach to causal inference. Counterfactuals and Causal Inference by Morgan and Winship focuses on social science applications. Targeted Learning by van der Laan and Rose offers a machine learning perspective on causal inference.

title: About OTTO Lab
text:
OTTO Lab (Observational Target Trial Operations) uses causal inference to address long-standing debates and real-world problems. Rigorous causal workflows clarify what works, for whom, when, and in which context - questions that matter for science, policy, and understanding cultural diversity.
We are based in the School of Psychological Sciences at Te Herenga Waka - Victoria University of Wellington, and is affiliated with the Centre for Applied Cross-Cultural Research (CACR).
We also maintain Places Map, an open research infrastructure for mapping places of worship and supporting cross-cultural policy research. The underlying codebase is available at github.com/go-bayes/places-of-worship.

title: About OTTO Lab
text:
Approach
We combine causal inference workflows with domain expertise to:

Identify and state clearly defined causal questions
Design studies that answer these questions
Clearly communicate findings

title: People
text:
Joseph Bulbulia



Director, OTTO Lab: 📧 joseph.bulbulia@vuw.ac.nz
🔗 University Profile Full CV
AboutOTTO Lab is based in the School of Psychological Sciences at Te Herenga Waka - Victoria University of Wellington.Joseph Bulbulia (Joe) teaches and researches in the School of Psychological Sciences at Victoria University of Wellington. His research investigates the complex drivers of human cooperation, conflict, and well-being, with a focus on the role of religion and values. Joseph specialises in methodologies for inferring causality from observational data. He also directs the Centre for Applied Cross-Cultural Research (CACR).Research Projects Joe contributes to two major longitudinal projects:
New Zealand Attitudes and Values Study (NZAVS): Joe serves as a principal investigator on major NZAVS projects. He uses 15 years of repeated-measures longitudinal data from more than 76,000 New Zealanders to investigate religion, social cohesion, and trust.
Pulotu Database of Pacific Religions: As a founding co-investigator, Joe uses this database of 116 Austronesian cultures to test theories about the evolution of religious beliefs and their effects on social behaviour.


Joe supervises students in a broad range of areas, including:

Personality and individual differences
Political psychology
Well-being/Flourishing
Religion (his primary interest)

Version 1.4.0 of the boilerplate R package was published on the Comprehensive R Archive Network (CRAN). The package supports reproducible management of standardised methods, results, measures, and report templates.

The second OTTO Lab article now in production is Religion, cooperation, and prosocial behavior: Methods and evidence for causality, by Michael McCullough, Don Davis, and Joseph Bulbulia. DOI

Taken together, the articles reflect OTTO Lab’s continuing work on religion, social behaviour, meaning, and resilience.




March 2026 | Georgia State University
It is with mixed feelings that we say goodbye to Dr Inkuk Kim, who has taken up a postdoctoral fellowship with Professor Don E. Davis at the HAPPI Lab at Georgia State University.
Inkuk remains a Fellow of OTTO Lab and is working on a number of projects related to environmental psychology, trust in science, and character formation over the adult lifespan.




20 February 2026 | Victoria University of Wellington
The Places Map project is now live at placesmap.org. Places Map is an open research infrastructure for mapping places of worship and supporting cross-cultural policy research.
Project code and workflows are available at github.com/go-bayes/places-of-worship.




January 2026 | Victoria University of Wellington
We are delighted to welcome two new PhD students to OTTO Lab: Mekonnen Tsehay and Mohammad Islam.
Mekonnen joins the lab from Ethiopia. He is estimating the causal effects of religious ritual behaviours on health and wellbeing among religiously identified people in New Zealand.
Mohammad joins the lab from Bangladesh. He is estimating the causal effects of Right-Wing Authoritarianism and Social Dominance Orientation on outcome-wide prejudice.
A warm welcome to Mekonnen and Mohammad.

title: OTTO Lab
text:
School of Psychological Sciences · Te Herenga Waka — Victoria University of Wellington



Observational Target Trial Operations


Observational causal inference for psychological science. Association does not imply causation. However, many of the really big questions can’t be addressed with experiments. Recent innovations in computer science, economics, and epidemiology reveal that under certain conditions, observational associations can support causal inferences. These methods are not widely employed in psychological science. We develop and apply causal inference methods to questions in psychological science. We also build research tools, teach these methods, and collaborate with investigators from around New Zealand and the World.

Target trial emulation  ·  NZAVS 2020–2023  ·  Lab report
Work Hours: The Body, Not the Mind
How work hours affect well-being: a target trial emulation in a national New Zealand cohort
Ballerina X. S. Chong · Chris G. Sibley · Joseph A. BulbuliaPLOS One · 2026

Longer work hours travel with poorer well-being, but an association cannot say what would happen if hours changed. We emulate the experiment we would like to run: among 24,579 pre-retirement New Zealanders, we estimate how 28 well-being outcomes would differ if the same cohort worked ten more or ten fewer hours each week than observed.


  24,579pre-retirement adults, NZAVS
  3annual waves, 2020–2023
  28well-being outcomes
  ±10hours per week, the two policies



The emulated trial

  
    What is our question?
    For pre-retirement New Zealand adults, how would 28 well-being outcomes differ one year later if weekly work hours shifted ten hours up, or ten hours down, from what would otherwise occur?
  
  
    What is our population?
    24,579 NZAVS participants of working age at baseline (2020/2021), followed across three annual waves to 2022/2023, with censoring adjustment carrying inference to the baseline cohort.
  
  
    What interventions do we compare?
    
      Shift up · +10 hours
      Weekly hours shifted ten upward, versus the natural course — the censoring-adjusted hours actually worked.
    
    
      Shift down · −10 hours
      Weekly hours shifted ten downward, versus the same natural course.
    
  




The central result
Shifting work hours affects recovery — fatigue, sleep, body mass — more clearly than well-being as a whole.
Under the upward shift, fatigue rises and sleep falls; body mass index and perceived physical health also worsen, though these estimates are more sensitive to residual confounding. Under the downward shift, the clearest fall is in fatigue. Most of the 28 outcomes change little under either policy, and the data better support the downward shift.


  
    +10 hours · the cost
    Recovery erodes
    Fatigue rises by 0.08 standard deviations and nightly sleep falls by roughly 3.4 minutes. Body mass index increases by roughly 0.19 kg/m² and perceived physical health declines by roughly 0.13 points, though both estimates are more sensitive to residual confounding. Perceived support rises slightly and carries the same caution.
  
  
    −10 hours · the relief
    Fatigue lifts first
    Fatigue falls by 0.04 standard deviations — the clearest change under the downward policy. Body mass index (−0.13 kg/m²) and perceived physical health (+0.07 points) also improve, and both estimates remain sensitive to residual confounding.
  




Inference & robustness

  
    01The natural course comparator
    Each policy is compared with the censoring-adjusted hours the cohort actually worked — not with a hypothetical zero-hours world, and not with each other.
  
  
    02Adjustment
    Modified treatment policy estimators, implemented in the lmtp R package, adjust for baseline differences and for dropout using machine learning.
  
  
    03Uncertainty, stated plainly
    Uncertainty remains substantial. Many point estimates attenuate towards zero after confounding control and censoring adjustment, and many Bonferroni-corrected intervals include zero.
  
  
    04Scope
    Estimates are defined for these shift policies in this population, and people gain and lose hours for many reasons. Both hours and outcomes are self-reported; random measurement error would likely attenuate true effects.
  




  Citation
  Chong, B. X. S., Sibley, C. G., & Bulbulia, J. A. (2026). How work hours affect well-being: A target trial emulation. PLOS One. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0350816
  Data: the New Zealand Attitudes and Values Study. Estimation: modified treatment policies with the lmtp R package.
